title: Bernstein-Vazirani: n classical queries vs 1 quantum query
problem_statement: Given oracle access to f(x) = s.x mod 2 (inner product over GF(2)) for a hidden n-bit string s, find s.

input.parameter: n = number of input bits of f.
input.size_measure: Query model: cost is the number of oracle calls. The harness materialises the 2^n-entry truth table only so that the oracle can be simulated.

algorithms.name: classical: query the unit vectors
algorithms.idea: f(e_i) is the i-th bit of s.
algorithms.time_complexity: n queries (optimal classically, also for randomized algorithms that succeed with probability > 1/2)

algorithms.name: Bernstein-Vazirani quantum algorithm
algorithms.idea: Hadamard transform, one phase-oracle query, Hadamard transform. The resulting state is exactly |s>.
algorithms.correctness: H^n sum_x (-1)^(s.x) |x> / sqrt(2^n) = |s> (Bernstein & Vazirani 1997). Deterministic: succeeds with probability 1.

lower_bounds.bound: n queries for every success probability > 1/2, randomized algorithms included
lower_bounds.source: Proved in this entry: for a uniformly random s, the answers s.x_1, ..., s.x_q to q queries (chosen adaptively) leave s uniform on the solutions of q linear equations over GF(2), an affine subspace of dimension >= n - q, so a deterministic q-query algorithm outputs s with probability at most 2^(q-n). Averaging over its coins, every randomized q-query algorithm also succeeds with probability at most 2^(q-n) on average over s, hence on some s; success > 1/2 on every s therefore needs q >= n. The problem is from Bernstein & Vazirani 1997

relationship: Proven separation in the query model: n classical queries vs 1 quantum query. It is only a linear (polynomial) gap. The recursive version of the problem (Bernstein & Vazirani 1997) gives a superpolynomial separation, and Simon's problem an exponential one (see simon-classical-vs-quantum).

verification.method: V1: both algorithms return s, which an independent check confirms against the full truth table, for n = 0..10 (quantum, simulated exactly with lib/qsim.py) and up to 16 (classical). V2 measures QUERY COUNTS reported through lib.qsim.Oracle: classical fits n exactly, and quantum is constant (1 query) for every n. Simulation time is exponential in n and is not the claim.

caveats: A separation relative to an oracle. It does not prove that quantum computers are more powerful for any explicit, efficiently computable function, and it does not imply BQP != BPP.
notes: Smallest example of a proven quantum query advantage; a building block of the recursive Fourier sampling separation.
